_scope: THIS PROJECT's use of a bench: which bench, what stands on it and where. Separate from the bench file on purpose - see bench.json's _scope.
_STATUS_2026_07_28: THE ARM MOVED AND IS NOW CLAMPED DOWN. Kyle relocated it from the return to the MAIN TABLE and fixed it in place, which satisfies 716.4's first invariant: everything expressed in base coordinates is only valid while the base cannot shift. The arm position below is MEASURED and is the new datum to build the cell around. THE CAMERAS ARE NOT: both were nulled out on this date because they were positioned for the old layout on the return and the arm is now on a different table, so every previously-measured camera number describes a geometry that no longer exists. They are also physically offline. Nulls mean `sim.simcam` will not draw them, which is correct - an invented pose renders a sight line that looks like evidence. Camera targets are in plan 713.9; the side camera also has no mount at all yet (717.5). What is NOT invalidated by any of this: camera INTRINSICS (a property of lens and sensor, not of position), the collision gate, IK, and the motion work.

arm._comment: Arm base centre, MEASURED 2026-07-28 by Kyle, clamped down. His words: 'on the main table, front edge, centered at 19.75 inches from the extent edge, the m1 center is 2.25in inset from the edge, arm is clamped down'. DERIVATION into this datum, written out because both axes had a plausible wrong reading. x CORRECTED 2026-07-28: the tape reading of 2.25 in put the back of the base 0.499 in PAST the table edge in the model, and Kyle confirmed 'yes its flush, assume my measurement was off a little so shift accordingly'. So x is now fixed by the FLUSH CONSTRAINT rather than by the tape: the base rear sits 69.82 mm (2.7487 in) behind the m1 axis (measured off the mesh), so a flush rear at the 27.5 in edge puts m1 at 27.5 - 2.7487 = 24.7513. That is a stiffer constraint than a tape to a rounded feature - the arm is physically registered against the edge, and the number now follows the geometry that made it flush. The original reading is kept here because it is the reason the error was findable at all. y = 82 - 19.75 = 62.25, measured from the table's FREE far end. The other reading of 'the extent edge' - 19.75 from y=0 - is ruled out twice over: y=0 is the SIDE WALL, not an edge you can put a tape on, and at y=19.75 the return surface is contiguous at x=27.5, so there would be no 'front edge' to inset 2.25 from. Both of Kyle's phrases only parse together at y=62.25.
arm._yaw_two_numbers: RE-DERIVED AGAIN 2026-07-31, and the guard caught it again. yaw_deg was 176.4796 (= 180 + reach_yaw -3.5204). Correcting j5's MOUNT OFFSET - the SO-101's gripper is fitted a quarter-turn from the model's zero, so the sim's jaws hung front-to-back while the arm's sit side by side - moved reach_yaw to -9.8841, because reach_yaw measures TOOL_BODY (the moving JAW) against BASE_BODY and rolling the wrist moves the jaw laterally. _selftest_arm_base_square failed with the base at -173.636 vs the measured 180. Nothing about the physical arm changed - it is still clamped square - which is exactly why the MEASURED angle (base_square_to_deg) is kept separate from the DERIVED one. Same cascade as the j1 mirror on 07-30, one joint over. TWO ANGLES, and confusing them put the arm 9.3 deg askew in the viewer until Kyle spotted it on 2026-07-28: 'the back edged of the base is parallel with the table edge, you have it off angle a few degrees'. `base_square_to_deg` is the MEASURABLE one - the bench direction the base is squared to, which is what a person actually sets when clamping it down. 180 = the back edge parallel to the table's front edge, arm facing the back wall. `yaw_deg` is what the code consumes, and by an old and deliberate convention it means the direction the arm REACHES at pan zero, which is NOT the same thing: this model reaches -3.5204 deg off its own base axis (Twin.reach_yaw_deg, because the SO-100 and SO-101 disagree by 90). NOT 'measured from the mesh', which this note used to say: reach_yaw_deg poses the arm at FRAME zero, so it runs through calibration.json's ratified j1 frame (zero_tick 2090, 82 ticks = 7.207 deg off rest) and through the tick->qpos map. That is precisely why it moved 12.819 deg on 2026-07-30 with no mesh change at all. Re-ratifying j1's zero_tick would move it again, and _selftest_arm_base_square would fail pointing at the arm model, which would not be what changed. So yaw_deg = 180 + -3.5204 = 176.4796. DERIVED, not measured - if the arm model is ever swapped, reach_yaw changes and this number is stale, which is why _selftest_arm_base_square asserts the built model's base really is square to base_square_to_deg and fails loudly if it drifts. RE-DERIVED 2026-07-30, and the guard is the reason it was caught: reach_yaw was +9.2983 until the twin's j1 mapping was found MIRRORED (plan 714.6 - the arm swings left at +45 and the twin put it right). Pan zero is measured in the same breath as the reach direction, so correcting j1's sign moved the reach by 12.819 deg and _selftest_arm_base_square failed with the base at -167.181 against the measured 180. Nothing about the physical arm changed - it is still clamped square - and that is exactly the point of keeping the MEASURED angle separate from the DERIVED one: the derived number absorbed the whole correction and the measured one never moved.
arm._xy_is_the_m1_axis: x/y locate the M1 AXIS (the shoulder_pan pivot), because that is the one feature on a real arm you can put a tape to and it is what Kyle measured. It is NOT the model's root body origin, which sits 38.8 mm away - attaching the model at these coordinates directly put the real pivot 1.5 in from where it was measured, which Kyle saw as 'a little bit in'. bench_scene now back-solves the attach origin from this axis via Twin.m1_offset_m. Base-relative checks cannot catch that class of error because they move with the arm.
arm._m1_height_reconciled: RESOLVED 2026-07-28, and the 'discrepancy' was mine, not Kyle's. He measured the centre of the m1 MOTOR at 2 in above the table top. I compared that against 62.4 mm and called it an 11.6 mm disagreement. 62.4 mm is the shoulder_pan JOINT ORIGIN - the point the kinematics rotate about - and this repo says 'm1 centre' when it means that joint origin, which is 18 mm away from the centre of the servo body. Kyle asked the right question: 'are you sure what you are checking against is the center?' It was not. Computed off the mesh at qpos 0, measured from the LOWEST base geometry (what a tape resting on the table actually reads): m1 servo body centre 46.5 mm = 1.83 in; joint origin 64.8 mm = 2.55 in. Against his 2.00 in the real gap is 4.3 mm, which is what reading a tape to the nearest inch on a 40 mm-tall motor looks like. The model and the bench agree; nothing was changed. SEPARATE ISSUE the check did expose: the base mesh's lowest point is 2.4 mm BELOW world z=0 while simcam asserts z=0 is the table, so the twin has the arm sunk 2.4 mm into the tabletop. Real, small, and left alone deliberately - see 716.4.

cameras.name: bench
cameras.notes: PLANNED, NOT MEASURED - drawn in amber so the intent can be looked at before anything is drilled (Kyle 2026-07-28: 'add the camera locations to the mujoco so I can see them and the LoS you intend'). Uses the ALREADY PRINTED 60 deg wall bracket on the back wall, on the arm's own line (along 62.25 = the arm's y), LENS 26.654 in above the top - the height that puts the optical axis exactly on the work-zone centre (x 17.35). STANDOFF IS NO LONGER A PLACEHOLDER: 1.961 in (49.8 mm) is computed from the printed bracket's own geometry, lens face to wall face, which is what the 2.0 in guess was standing in for - it landed within 1 mm, but the height depends on it (h = (17.35 - standoff) * tan 60), so it needed to be real. INSTALL: the SCREW HOLES go 57.3 mm (2.26 in) ABOVE the lens height, i.e. 28.91 in above the table top, because the lens hangs below the plate on this bracket - 19.05 mm proud of the PCB along the axis, and at 60 deg most of that becomes drop. Alternative: the 45 deg bracket at a lens height of 15.4 in, which trades 30 deg off nadir for 45 but gains resolution (2.33 vs 1.65 px/mm). WHY THE BACK WALL: the arm reaches toward it, so targets are always between the camera and the arm, and the arm cannot occlude them at the moment of grasp - the failure a true overhead view has. Clears the shelf (underside 36.5) by ~10 in, and sits 578 mm from m1 against a 376 mm reach, so the arm cannot strike it. POSITION RETIRED 2026-07-28, not lost - see _STATUS_2026_07_28. It was on the SIDE wall at along 51.5, lens centre z 29.0 above the top, tilted 60 deg down, standoff never measured; the z was genuinely measured on 2026-07-26. Those numbers are kept here as history and must not be reinstated: they placed the camera relative to an arm that stood on the RETURN, and the arm is now on the main table roughly 42 in away, so the old pose points at empty bench. Nulled rather than adjusted because there is no arithmetic that turns a measurement of the old layout into a measurement of the new one. Re-measure after mounting; targets are in 713.9 (overhead: ~504 mm above the table, near-nadir, centred on the work zone - which is LOWER than the 29 in it was at). Registry entry for the live camera is cameras.json - this is only where it is in space.

cameras.name: low
cameras.notes: PLANNED, NOT MEASURED - amber in the viewer. FREE-STANDING rather than on a wall: the 717.5 stand bolted to the OUTSIDE SHORT EDGE of the main table (Kyle 2026-07-28: 'mounted on the outside short edge of the main table, whatever depth is best, I was thinking centered with a perpendicular angle'). CORRECTED from an earlier placement on the long front edge at x=27.5, which was my misreading of which edge - the short edge is better on every count and needs no yaw at all. x=13.75 is the CENTRE of that 27.5 in edge, yaw 270 looks straight down the table, perpendicular to the edge the plate is bolted to, so the printed part is symmetric. HEIGHT AND ANGLE DECIDED 2026-07-28 (Kyle: 'the height and angle are for you to decide ... make some interim decision ... use your best judgement for now'): LENS 75 mm above the top, 7 deg down. y=80.409 rather than 82.0 because the PLATE bolts to the y=82 face and the lens sits 40.4 mm inboard of it - the lens is 19.05 mm proud of the PCB (Kyle measured; no published figure exists for this module), so the optical centre is NOT the board and placing the board at 75 would have left the real lens low and forward. WHY 7 DEG: steep enough that the practical fixture zone stays inside the bottom of the frame, shallow enough to leave headroom for a lifted part. Table is in frame from y 75.24 outward, so everything within 300 mm of the arm base (y 74.06 and below) is covered with 1.18 in to spare; only the last 1.81 in of the arm's extreme lateral reach, 3 in from the lens, falls outside. Across the fixture zone it sees the table plus 127-291 mm of height above it, at 6.94 px/mm near and 1.68 px/mm far (40 mm tag: 278 px down to 67 px). WHY CENTRED RATHER THAN ALIGNED WITH THE WORK ZONE (x=17.35, which would put the axis dead on it): coverage absorbs the 3.6 in offset entirely at the distances that matter, the resolution difference is 2.52 vs 2.57 px/mm, and centring buys 38 mm more clearance from the arm - 574 mm from m1 against a 376 mm reach, so the arm cannot strike it by a wide margin. CAVEAT, because 'covers the work zone' is only true where it matters: this is a wide-angle lens looking down a long table, so it sees a WEDGE - at the arm's own line (~20 in away) the frame is 761 mm and spans the whole table depth, but the nearest work-zone rows at y~77 are only 5 in away and are seen only in a narrow strip. Those rows are the arm's extreme lateral reach and are rarely worked. Focus the barrel LAST, at the real fixture distance, once 716.4 places the nest. SECOND CAMERA, added 2026-07-27. Position has never been measured and stays NULL - the sim will not draw it, which is correct behaviour rather than a gap: an invented pose renders a sight line that looks like evidence. NAME AND ROLE ARE STILL PROVISIONAL, taken from what its first frame showed rather than from Kyle. It has NO MOUNT AT ALL (717.5) and is currently offline. Target from 713.9: ~90 deg azimuth from the arm's reach axis, ~268 mm standoff, 100-200 mm above the table - never on the base side looking down the reach axis, where the arm blocks everything it reaches for. Worth keeping a low angle wherever it lands: the overhead camera cannot resolve HEIGHT above the table and this one can, which is what a grasp approach needs, and it is the only fixed viewpoint that still sees the target when the arm reaches over it.
